units.translation: Etym. M. p. 103, 48 posits θελεμός [willing] as the primitive form of the word ἐθελημός [willing]. Arcad. p. 61, 3: τὸ δὲ θελεμός ἀπὸ τοῦ θελημός ὀξύνεται [but θελεμός is accented on the ultima, from θελημός]. Hesiod Op. 118 used ἐθελημός in the sense of 'voluntary' of the race of men before Prometheus: οἱ δ᾽ ἐθελημοὶ ἥσυχοι ἔργα νέμοντο [and they, willing and at peace, tended their works], and others cited in the Thesaurus vol. 3 p. 171, and Aeschylus in the same sense Suppl. 1028: ποταμοὺς δ᾽, οἳ διὰ χώρας θελεμὸν πῶμα χέουσιν [and rivers, which pour a willing drink through the land]. But at Sept. 707, if Conington correctly conjectured θελεμωτέρω πνεύματι [with a calmer breath] for θαλερωτέρῳ πνεύματι [with a more vigorous breath], it is said rather in the sense of 'quiet'. In Hesychius there is θέλεμον: οἰκτρὸν, ἥσυχον [pitiable, quiet], and θελέμως: ἡσύχως, οἰκτρῶς [quietly, pitiably], where the interpretations οἰκτρόν [pitiable] and οἰκτρῶς [pitiably] are strange. Moreover, in the verse of Aeschylus Haupt conjectured the same as Conington in the Index of Lectures, Berlin summer 1865.
but θελεμός is accented on the ultima, from θελημός; ἐθελημός
and they, willing and at peace, tended their works
and rivers, which pour a willing drink through the land
soothing and charm of my tongue
a bed as a charm for toils
having the power of soothing or charming
having the power of soothing or charming
may a soothing word come from a word
the soothing shaft of the eye
thus Bothius for θεακτορι [to the goddess?], which is without accent in M
nothing is denied to enchanting Persuasion

There are two forms of this verb, ἐθέλω [to be willing], which we have discussed in its place, and θέλω [to be willing], which the tragedians use especially in iambic trimeters, where the other form ἐθέλω is generally inconvenient. The aorist imperative, optative, subjunctive, and participle θέλησον [be willing], θελήσαιμι [may I be willing], θελήσω [I will be willing], and θελήσας [having been willing] are taken from the disyllabic form, but the indicative is not ἐθέλησα, but ἠθέλησα from the other form ἐθέλω. On the distinction between θέλω and βούλομαι [to wish] see under that word. They differ in that the verb θέλω contains the notion of inclination, the verb βούλομαι of counsel and deliberation, although this distinction is often neglected and one is frequently used for the other, as I have said in the Lexicon Sophocleum p. 219.
Thus I corrected what is in M: οὐ δοῦναι θέλει [he is not willing to give]: see Preface to the fifth Leipzig edition p. LXXIII.
where Casaubon rightly, as it seems, restored ναυστολοῦσ᾽ [sailing].
those willing to cast out Cronus from his seat
I want to advise you the best things
do you want to take other things in addition
if you are willing even to toil
I would wish that the greatest number might meet with misfortunes
not willing to babble in vain
he wants to join in Cypris
